questions.stem:
Consider the following code segment.

```text
x ← 3
total ← 0
REPEAT 6 TIMES
{
   x ← x + 1
   IF (x MOD 2 = 0)
   {
      total ← total + x
   }
}
DISPLAY (total)
```

What is displayed as a result of running the code segment?

options.why: Correct. x goes from 4 to 9; the multiples of 2 among them are added.
total adds the values, not 1 each time.
Recheck which values are multiples of 2.
Only values divisible by 2 are added.

questions.explanation: The values of x are 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9; the multiples of 2 add to 18.

questions.stem: Why might a programmer use a heuristic to plan delivery routes through hundreds of stops?

options.text: Heuristics always find the best possible route
options.why: They find an approximate solution.
They still compute a solution.
It is decidable but slow.

options.text: Finding the guaranteed best route would take unreasonable time, so a good-enough route found quickly is preferred
options.why: Correct. Heuristics trade optimality for speed.

questions.explanation: Heuristics trade optimality for speed.

questions.stem:
The following code segment is intended to display the sum of the values in `nums`.

```text
FOR EACH n IN nums
{
   total ← 0
   total ← total + n
}
DISPLAY (total)
```

What is displayed when `nums` is `[9, 16, 6, 3]`, and why?

options.why: total is set back to 0 before each addition.

options.text: 0, because total is reset after the loop
options.why: The reset happens before the addition in each pass.

options.text: 3, because total is reset to 0 on every pass
options.why: Correct. The reset inside the loop discards the earlier values.

options.text: 9, because the loop stops after one pass
options.why: FOR EACH visits every element.

questions.explanation: Each pass sets total to 0 and then adds n, so only the last value, 3, remains. Moving `total ← 0` before the loop fixes it.

questions.stem:
Consider the following code segment.

```text
nums ← [23, 8, 9, 15]
APPEND(nums, 37)
INSERT(nums, 2, 61)
REMOVE(nums, 5)
DISPLAY (nums)
```

What is displayed as a result of running the code segment?

options.why: INSERT adds a new element; it does not replace one.
INSERT and REMOVE also change the list.
Correct. List indexes start at 1; INSERT shifts later elements right and REMOVE shifts them left.
AP pseudocode lists start at index 1, not 0.

questions.explanation: After APPEND: [23, 8, 9, 15, 37]. INSERT at 2 and REMOVE at 5 give [23, 61, 8, 9, 37].

questions.stem: A procedure `countAbove(list)` should return how many values in list are greater than 11, but the programmer suspects it uses ≥ instead of >. Which test input would reveal this error?

options.why: Every value is above 11, so both versions return the same count.
No value equals 11, so both versions agree.
Correct. It contains 11, which ≥ counts but > does not, so the two versions give different results.
No value is 11 or above, so both versions return 0.

questions.explanation: Only an input containing the boundary value 11 makes ≥ and > behave differently.

options.why: 24 is greater than 23, so -1 is never reached.
The procedure returns the item, not its index.
RETURN stops the procedure immediately; later values are not checked.
Correct. RETURN ends the procedure at the first value greater than the limit.

questions.stem: A data set from a school library contains one row per transaction with these fields: book title, genre, checkout date, return date. Which question can be answered using only this data?

options.text: Which grade level borrows the most books?
options.why: The data does not include borrower grade.
The data does not include ratings.

options.text: What is the average number of days a book is kept?
options.why: Correct. Every field it needs is in the data set.

options.text: How much did each book cost the library?
options.why: The data does not include purchase price.

questions.explanation: Only "What is the average number of days a book is kept?" can be answered from the listed fields; each other question needs data that was not collected.

questions.stem: A network has computers P, Q, R, S, T, U. The direct connections are: P–T, P–U, Q–S, R–T, R–U, S–T, S–U, T–U. What is the minimum number of connections that must fail for computer S to be unable to communicate with computer P?

options.why: After that many failures a path still remains.
Correct. Removing 2 well-chosen connections separates S from P; removing fewer always leaves a path.
Some set of 2 connections already disconnects them.
Not every connection needs to fail.

questions.explanation: S has 3 connections and P has 2. Checking failures systematically shows that 2 is the fewest that leaves no path between them.
